title: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, and the pillar of fire with no end either way. Stay awake for what matters. Now the festival weeks are done, and the lineage track begins.

Short enough to fit on a postcard: that's the Isha Upanishad. In year one you read it as ideas. This time, read it as a life: how someone who has to work, earn, raise children and pay rent might actually live it. It belongs to the first of three roads the tradition describes for a life, and this week, the end of year two, each road gets a short walk: karma, the way of action; bhakti, the way of love; jnana, the way of knowing. First, action.

segments.voice: Start with the word. Karma comes from the Sanskrit root kri, to do. Its plain meaning is action, a deed; the teachings about deeds bearing fruit, and lives following lives, are built around that plain center. On the path of karma, the question isn't how to escape action, but how to act well. Now the Isha's first verse. It opens: Isha vasyam idam sarvam. All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is to be dwelt in by the Lord, or, in another reading, clothed by the Lord. Then two short commands. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: enjoy by what is let go, or, as others read it, enjoy what has been given. And ma gridhah: do not covet. Then a question: kasya svid dhanam. Whose, after all, is wealth? Commentators read the middle line differently. Shankara, the teacher of non-dual Vedanta, hears renunciation in it: give up the sense of owning, and you're free. Others hear something closer to gratitude: take what you're given, as given, and enjoy it without grabbing for more. Both readings meet in the same place. You can live fully in the world, eat, work, enjoy, as long as you don't treat it as yours to hoard. Gandhi is reported to have said that if every other scripture were lost and only this verse survived, Hinduism would still live. For a working life, the verse offers an unusual and practical posture: hold everything you have the way you'd hold something borrowed.
screen: `KARMA: FROM KRI, TO DO.` · `ALL THIS IS DWELT IN BY THE LORD.` · `ENJOY BY LETTING GO. DON'T COVET.` · `WHOSE IS WEALTH?` · then, large: `HOLD IT LIKE SOMETHING BORROWED.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and bring to mind a few things you think of as yours: your phone, your home, your time, your body. Hold each one in mind and ask the verse's question, whose is this, really, without answering in words. Notice if your grip loosens a little, then rest with open hands.
Karma. Action, from the root to do. The Isha's first verse asks you to act and enjoy in a world that isn't yours to own.
Your line: whose, after all, is wealth? Tomorrow, the verse that says keep working. Day six hundred ninety.

howItsDone: The Isha's opening verse is recited by some Hindus at the start of study or a talk, and teachers of karma yoga often cite it as a posture for working life: act and enjoy without the sense of owning.

original.note: Sanskrit karman (karma): action, deed, from the root kṛ, to do.

what a scholar hears: Isha 1 can be read as renunciation (Shankara) or as enjoying what is allotted; the word vāsyam in īśā vāsyam can mean dwelt in or covered by the Lord.

chat.says: Does following the Isha Upanishad mean giving away everything you own?
options: Not necessarily: enjoy what you have, but don't covet it. Hold it like a loan.
Yes, the verse tells everyone to leave home and live in the forest.
No, it says wealth is yours for keeps, as long as you earned it.
chat.meaning: The Isha's first verse says enjoy by letting go and do not covet: whose, after all, is wealth? Readings differ, but none treats wealth as yours to hoard.
